deckName: KS3 DT · J2 Lesson 3 — Chatbot Workshop (Teacher Deck)

slides.kicker: OUR LADY'S GRAMMAR SCHOOL · DIGITAL TECHNOLOGY
slides.heading: Lesson 3 · Chatbot Workshop
slides.sub: Your program asks. Somebody answers. — J2 · Lesson 3 of 17
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: coming in, logging in, opening the class link from Google Classroom. The lesson does not open on today's work — it opens on the Do-Now, a short set of questions from the last two lessons that mark themselves as each pupil answers them. Nothing in it is graded and nothing about it is shown to the class.

SAY: "Log in, open the class link, and work through the warm-up on your own screen. When it hands you over to today's first card, stop and look up."

WHY: it is revision, and it gives you a settled room to take the register in.

WHEN TO MOVE: when most of the room is sitting on today's first card, stop everybody, eyes front, and go on.

slides.heading: In this lesson you will…
bullets: Make a program stop and wait for somebody to type something.
Keep what was typed, and use it later in the same program.
Write a chatbot of your own, in your own words.
Test somebody else's chatbot, and write down what you found.
slides.notes:
SAY these as they are written. All four are things she will have DONE by the end of the hour, not things she will have heard about.

WHY IT MATTERS: every program these pupils have written so far did exactly the same thing every time it ran. From today a program can do something different depending on what a person types into it. That is the whole hour in one sentence, and it is worth saying out loud.

WHEN TO MOVE: straight on.

slides.heading: The one new idea today
bullets: A program can STOP in the middle and wait for a person.
Whatever that person types is kept in a name, like any other value.
The rest of the program can then use it.
Nothing else about writing Python changes today.
slides.notes:
SAY: "There is one new idea today and everything else is what you already do. A program can stop halfway through, wait for somebody to type something, and then carry on using whatever was typed."

DO NOT put the word input( ) on the board yet. The film shows it happening before it is named, and a pupil who has seen it happen understands the word when it arrives. Naming it here costs you that.

WHEN TO MOVE: straight on.

slides.heading: How the hour is laid out
bullets: A short film on your own screen, then three training builds.
Then twelve minutes writing a chatbot that is yours.
Then you swap: you test a partner's bot and they test yours.
Two short screens at the end, and both are quick.
slides.notes:
SAY it as written. Pupils work far better when they know the shape of the hour, and the Swap in particular is easier to run if the room already knows it is coming.

WHEN TO MOVE: straight on.

slides.heading: Two things before we start
bullets: Everything you write today is read by somebody else in this room.
So write your bot's words the way you would speak to a person here.
Nothing you type is marked for spelling.
If your program stops with a red message, that is normal. Read the plain line underneath it.
slides.notes:
SAY the first two as a pair, and mean them. The Swap is the reason: a pupil's own sentences will be read by a classmate within the hour, and saying so now is worth more than any rule said afterwards.

SAY: "If your program stops and Python puts up a message, that is not you being told off. Every one of those messages has a plain English line under it saying what to look at. Read that line."

WHEN TO MOVE: straight on to the film slide, then let them go.

slides.heading: The film — on your own screen
bullets: It plays on your own computer, not on the board.
It has no sound, so every word you need is written on the screen.
It is in three parts, and the buttons underneath jump to any part.
The film lasts just over four minutes. Watch it once, then move on to the next card.
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: about to start the film on their own machines, headphones not needed.

SAY: "The film is on your screen, not mine. It has no sound at all, so you will not miss anything if the room is noisy. Just over four minutes. Watch it once and then keep going. Everything the film shows is written again on the cards after it, so you will not lose anything by moving on."

WHAT THEY WILL SEE: a player with three buttons under it, named "What a chatbot really is", "The program stops and waits" and "Reading the whole program". A pupil can jump to any part while she is on this screen.

DO NOT play it on the board. It is written to be read at each pupil's own pace, and reading it as a class removes the pausing that makes it work.

WHILE IT RUNS: these four minutes are your chance to walk the room and check everybody is actually on it.

WHEN TO MOVE: when most of the room is past it — the build cards explain themselves, so the stragglers can catch up there.

slides.heading: STOP — eyes front · The training builds
bullets: Three builds, and they get harder as you go.
The first one is already written: read it and run it.
The second is in pieces and you put it in order.
The third has gaps in it and you fill them in.
Every one of them RUNS. If it stops, read the plain line under the red.
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: film finished, eyes front. One minute here saves you ten walking the room.

SAY: "Three training builds, and they get harder. The first one is already written for you — read it, run it, and watch what happens when it asks you something. The second one is in pieces and you put the pieces in order. The third has gaps and you fill them."

THEN SAY: "All three of them actually run. When you press RUN the program does what it says, including stopping and waiting for you."

DO NOT walk anybody through build three from the front. It is the one that is marked, and it is meant to be worked out.

WHEN TO MOVE: next slide, then send them in.

slides.heading: What a build screen looks like
bullets: The program is on the left. The console — where it talks — is on the right.
RUN is at the bottom. Nothing happens until it is pressed.
When the program asks a question, a box appears and the program waits.
Type an answer, press the button, and the program carries on.
slides.notes:
SAY it while the picture is up, pointing at each part. Most of the questions you will be asked in the next ten minutes are answered by this slide.

WHAT THEY WILL SEE: the picture is the first build the moment its bot has asked its question — the program on the left, the conversation and the reply space on the right, and RUN switched off until the answer is sent.

THE ONE TO STRESS: the program WAITS. A pupil who does not realise the program has stopped on purpose thinks it has crashed.

WHEN TO MOVE: send them in. Walk the room.

slides.heading: When Python stops
bullets: If Python stops, the console goes red and shows Python's own words.
Under them is one line in plain English saying what to look at.
Read that line first. It tells you which line of your program to check.
A stopped run costs you nothing. Fix the line and press RUN again.
The first build stops on purpose. The mistake is in there for you to find.
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: about to press RUN on the first build, which has a mistake planted in it on purpose.

SAY it with the picture up: "When your program stops, this is what you see. Python's own words come first. The line under them is in plain English, and it tells you what to look at. Read that line first."

WHAT THEY WILL SEE: the picture is the console after the first build's planted mistake — Python's own error words, and the plain line underneath. The two always appear together. The plain line is the one to point at.

THE ONE TO STRESS: a stopped run is not a failure and costs nothing. Build 1 stops on purpose — the wrong word is planted — so every pupil meets this screen in the first two minutes and knows what it means before she meets it on her own bot.

THE HELP THAT ACTUALLY HELPS — three questions, in this order: What did the console print? What did you want it to print? Which one line are you going to change? You do not need to know any Python to ask those, and they are worth more than an answer would be.

WHEN TO MOVE: straight on.

slides.heading: The lines are in the wrong order
bullets: In Training build 3 you get the lines out of order. The order on the left is not a hint. You work out the correct order yourself.
Click a line to move it into Your program, or drag it.
Some lines have gaps in them. You type your own words into the gaps.
To take a line back, press the button beside it that says Put this line back.
RUN switches on as soon as there is at least one line in Your program.
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: about to open the third training build, the one that carries the first badge.

SAY it with the picture up, pointing at each part: "The lines are on the left, and your program is on the right. The lines come up in a different order every time, so the order on the left is not a hint. You work out the correct order yourself."

WHAT THEY WILL SEE: the picture is the third build before a line has been moved — the shuffled lines with their gaps, the empty program, and the RUN button still switched off.

THE ONE TO STRESS: the platform shuffles the lines afresh every time the card opens, for every pupil — the screen does not announce this, but it is true — so two neighbours see different orders, and the position of a line on the next desk tells her nothing. That is worth saying out loud, kindly, once.

WHILE THEY WORK: a line can be added by clicking it instead of dragging it, which is worth saying to anyone struggling with the mouse. To take a line back she presses the button beside it that says Put this line back; clicking the line itself does nothing.

WHEN TO MOVE: send them in. Walk the room.

slides.heading: STOP — eyes front · Your own bot
bullets: Twelve minutes. The bot is yours and every word in it is yours.
It has to ask two things and use BOTH answers before it finishes.
First, watch the film on the card called Your bot. It lasts just over two minutes.
You can use the four ready-made lines on the card. The name on each line tells you what that line does. Using them is not cheating.
Somebody in this room is going to read every word you write.
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: the three training builds finished, eyes front. This is the biggest single block of the hour and the room needs to know what "finished" looks like before it starts.

SAY: "Twelve minutes. You are writing a chatbot and every word it says is yours. There are only two rules: it has to ask two things, and it has to use both answers before it finishes."

THEN SAY: "There is a short film on that card and I want you to watch it first. It shows the two things people get stuck on."

THEN SAY, and say it plainly: "Somebody else in this room is going to run your bot in about fifteen minutes and read every word of it. Write it for them."

ABOUT THE READY-MADE LINES: there are four, each named by the job it does, and a pupil who cannot start can click one and it lands in her program with the words still to change. Tell the room the ready-made lines are there, and that using them is not cheating — the words are still hers.

WHEN TO MOVE: next slide, then twelve minutes of walking the room.

slides.heading: First you plan
bullets: You see the PLAN first. It shows the goal, the film, and the three jobs. The jobs are in the order you do them.
Watch the film on the card before you type anything. It lasts just over two minutes.
Press the button marked Start writing. The card turns into the page where you type.
slides.notes:
SAY, with the picture up: "The card starts by telling you what your bot has to do — three jobs, in order. There is a short film on it, and I want you to watch that first. When you press Start writing, the card turns into the page where you type, and those same three jobs move up to the top so you can see them the whole time."

WHAT THEY WILL SEE: the picture is the PLAN face — the goal, the film, the three jobs, and the Start writing button. Nothing can be typed on this face, and that is deliberate: she reads what the bot has to do before she can start.

WHEN TO MOVE: next slide.

slides.heading: Then you type
bullets: Your three jobs sit along the top of the page.
You type in the black space underneath. There is room for as many lines as you need.
Four ready-made lines sit under the black space. The name on each line tells you what that line does. Click one and it lands in your program.
The three jobs tick only after you press RUN. Each job ticks if your bot really does that job.
slides.notes:
SAY, with the picture up, pointing at each part: "Your three jobs are along the top. You type in the black space underneath. The four ready-made lines are under it, and clicking one puts it into your program."

WHAT THEY WILL SEE: the picture is the page where she types, before a character has been typed — the three jobs along the top, the empty box, and the four ready-made lines under it.

THE ONE TO STRESS: the three jobs are not read off her program. They watch her program while it RUNS. So a pupil who has written the right thing but not pressed RUN still sees "not checked yet" beside every job, and that is correct rather than broken.

IF SHE ASKS why it will not tick: "Have you run it since you changed it?" answers most of it.

ABOUT THE READY-MADE LINES: using them is not cheating — the words are still hers to change.

The card deliberately shows one thing at a time. The conversation and the console are not on the page when she arrives. They appear when she presses RUN — the console first, saying it is running, and the conversation the first time her bot asks something.

WHEN TO MOVE: send them in.

slides.heading: STOP — eyes front · The Swap
bullets: You are about to be given a partner. The website chooses.
You are not told who they are, and they are not told who you are.
You each get a call sign — Spanner 7, Chisel 3 — and that is what you are.
You run their bot. They run yours. Then you each write a short report.
The report goes to them. Write the one you would want back.
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: bots written, eyes front. THIS SLIDE IS THE ONE TO SLOW DOWN ON, especially the first time you run a paired activity.

SAY: "In a moment the website is going to pair you with somebody else in this room. You do not choose, and I do not choose — it pairs whoever is ready at the same time."

THEN SAY: "You are not told who your partner is and they are not told who you are. You are each given a call sign instead — you might be Spanner 7 and they might be Chisel 3. The screen tells you yours. Use it."

THEN SAY: "You run their bot, they run yours, and then you each write a short report back. Write the report you would want to get."

WHY NO REAL NAMES: an honest report is much easier to write, and much easier to read, when neither pupil knows whose it is. Say that out loud — pupils find it reassuring rather than strange.

IF THE CLASS IS AN ODD NUMBER: the website holds the last three pupils and puts them in one group of three, so nobody is left waiting for a partner who is not coming. You do not have to do anything.

IF SOMEBODY IS STILL WAITING: they are not stuck, and they do not need you. A cartoon chatbot called Fred keeps them company, and after a short wait the screen itself offers "Test my own bot instead" — which takes that pupil through the whole Swap alone, on their own bot, badge included. The same offer appears for a pupil whose partner's bot never arrives. Nothing on this screen needs a teacher to release it, which is what makes it safe on a cover day.

WHEN TO MOVE: next slide, then send them in.

slides.heading: While you wait
bullets: You might have to wait for a partner. Nothing is wrong: stay on this screen.
While you wait, a cartoon chatbot called Fred keeps you company. Talk to him if you like.
The moment somebody is ready, the screen changes by itself.
Have you been waiting a while? The screen offers you a button to test your own bot instead.
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: bots finished at different times, so pupils reach the Swap at different times — the first ones through will wait.

SAY it with the picture up: "If you get this screen, you are in the queue and nothing is wrong. The website pairs whoever is ready at the same time. Fred is there to talk to while you wait."

WHAT THEY WILL SEE: the picture is the waiting card, with Fred on it. Fred is a chatbot, and the card says so — he is not a pupil.

IF SOMEBODY IS STILL WAITING: they do not need you. After a longer wait the screen itself offers "Test my own bot instead", which takes that pupil through the whole Swap alone, on her own bot, badge included. Nothing on this screen needs a teacher to release it.

WHEN TO MOVE: next slide.

slides.heading: You have a partner
bullets: This card appears the moment the website has found you a partner.
The screen tells you your partner's call sign. It also tells you what you are called on their screen.
Real names stay secret — theirs and yours. Keep them out of anything you type.
Press Start the Swap. Your bot goes to them, and theirs comes to you.
slides.notes:
SAY it with the picture up: "This is the card you get when you have a partner. It tells you their call sign and yours. That is the only name either of you sees. Press Start the Swap."

WHAT THEY WILL SEE: the picture is the PARTNER FOUND card, with two call signs on it — hers, and her partner's. The names on the picture are examples: every pair gets its own.

THE ONE TO STRESS: real names stay out of everything typed, including her own. You can see who is paired with whom on the Live tab, by call sign with real names in brackets.

WHEN TO MOVE: next slide.

slides.heading: What the Swap looks like
bullets: First you are in the tester's seat: their bot runs on your screen, exactly as they wrote it.
You answer its questions like anybody would.
When their bot has finished, the button marked Write the report turns on.
There are two spaces: one for a thing that worked, and one for a thing you would change.
Then you swap seats. They test your bot while you watch every line, and their report on YOUR bot comes back to you.
slides.notes:
SAY, with the picture up: "First you are the tester. Your partner's bot runs on your screen. Answer it like anybody would, and when it has finished, write the report."

WHAT THEY WILL SEE: the picture is the tester's seat — a partner's bot running on her screen, mid-conversation, with the reply space waiting for her answer.

THE ONE TO STRESS: they are TESTING, not marking. The report is two short spaces, one sentence in each: one thing that worked, and one thing they would change. It is not a grade, and there is no score anywhere on the screen.

TWO WAITS THAT ARE NOT FAULTS: when a pupil presses Send my report, the screen says "Sending your report…" for a moment while it travels. Then she waits for her partner's report about her bot, which arrives a few seconds after her partner presses Send my report. Neither wait is a freeze.

WHAT YOU CAN SEE, on your own screen: open the class link yourself and sign in with your staff account — the same address the pupils use opens the teacher's view for a staff login. Click its Live tab. The Pairing panel there shows who is paired with whom, by call sign with real names in brackets, and its Channel button opens what a pair has actually sent each other. Use it if you need it — and tell the class it exists. A pupil who knows that the teacher can read the messages writes a better report.

WHEN TO MOVE: send them in. This runs about eleven minutes.

slides.heading: The last two screens
bullets: First a screen of three extra jobs. They are optional and none of them is marked.
Then one question about what input( ) does. That one IS marked.
You are told whether you were right, and why, at the very end.
Then How did it go? — two ratings and a private line to me.
Nobody leaves without finishing that one.
slides.notes:
SAY: "One marked question at the end. You are told whether you were right, and why, at the very end of the lesson — after the How did it go? screen."

ABOUT THE COMMENT BOX on the How did it go? screen: it goes to you and to nobody else. Pupils use it properly when they are told that plainly.

WHAT THEY WILL SEE: the picture is the extra-jobs screen — three jobs, none of them ticked, and the button at the bottom that carries her straight on.

EXTRA JOBS: every pupil lands on the extra-jobs screen after the Swap — it is not a reward for finishing early. There are three of them, they are worth no points at all, nothing there is marked or saved, and there is a button to carry straight on. Say so — a pupil who thinks she is missing marks will rush the ones that matter.

WHEN TO MOVE: straight on to the closer.

slides.heading: Before you leave
bullets: Finish How did it go? Nobody leaves without it.
Sign out every time. Anything the next person does looks like you.
Your bot is saved. It will still be there next lesson.
slides.notes:
SAY the sign-out line every lesson without exception. On shared C2k machines it is the single habit that matters most.

SAY: "Your bot is saved. You do not need to write it down or email it to yourself."

LAST THING: if the room has been noisy about the Swap, it is worth one sentence — "the reports you wrote each other were better than I expected" — said honestly. It sets up the next paired lesson.
